**Christ the Redeemer (Cristo Redentor) on Corcovado**
The 98-foot (30 m) Art Deco statue of Jesus with outstretched arms, made of reinforced concrete and soapstone and completed in 1931. It was designed by the French sculptor Paul Landowski and stands atop Corcovado Mountain. It was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World and was renovated in 1980 ahead of Pope John Paul II's visit.

**Sugarloaf Mountain (Pão de Açúcar)**
A granite peak on a peninsula at the mouth of Guanabara Bay, separating the bay from the Atlantic Ocean. Tourists reach its summit by cable car, and it is one of the city's two iconic peaks along with Corcovado.

**Copacabana and Ipanema beaches**
Famous beaches in the affluent South Zone. Copacabana runs along the seafront boulevard Avenida Atlântica. Ipanema names the bossa nova standard "The Girl from Ipanema." Nearby beach neighborhoods include Leme, which has a seated statue of the writer Clarice Lispector, Leblon, the surf spot Arpoador, and Botafogo.

**Tijuca Forest**
A hand-replanted rainforest, part of Tijuca National Park, often called one of the world's largest urban forests (along with the city's Pedra Branca forest). It surrounds Corcovado and includes the granite monolith Pedra da Gávea and the stone slab called the Mesa do Imperador ("Emperor's Table"). The upscale beach district of Barra da Tijuca shares its name.

**Favelas: Rocinha, Complexo do Alemão and others**
Rio's hillside shantytowns are called favelas. Rocinha is among the largest in Brazil, and others include Morro da Providência (often called the first favela), Complexo do Alemão ("Complex of the German"), and Babilônia.

**Cidade de Deus (City of God)**
A western favela that gave its name to the acclaimed 2002 crime film City of God, directed by Fernando Meirelles. Barack Obama visited the neighborhood during his 2011 trip to Brazil.

**Maracanã Stadium**
Rio's famous soccer stadium, once the largest in the world. It hosted the World Cup finals of 1950 and 2014. Clubs such as Fluminense and Flamengo play there.

**Guanabara Bay and the Rio–Niterói Bridge**
Rio lies on the western shore of Guanabara Bay. An eight-mile (13 km) bridge crosses the bay to Niterói, and São Gonçalo is also on the far side. The international airport is on Governador Island in the bay, and the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro's main campus is on Fundão Island.

**Cariocas and fluminenses**
Residents of the city are called cariocas, a word of Tupi origin. People from the surrounding state of Rio de Janeiro are called fluminenses, a word that also names the Fluminense soccer club.

**2016 Summer Olympics**
Rio hosted the 2016 Summer Olympics, the first Olympic Games held in South America.

**Carnival and the Sambadrome**
Rio's pre-Lenten Carnival is often called the biggest in the world. Its centerpiece is the samba school parade in the Sambadrome, a purpose-built parade avenue with grandstands designed by Oscar Niemeyer.

**Former capital of Brazil**
Rio was Brazil's capital until 1960, when the government moved to the newly built Brasília. The city then formed the separate state of Guanabara until it merged into Rio de Janeiro state in 1975. It is Brazil's second-largest city after São Paulo and is nicknamed the "Marvelous City" (Cidade Maravilhosa).

**Selarón Steps**
A staircase linking the Lapa and Santa Teresa neighborhoods, covered in colorful tiles by the Chilean-born artist Jorge Selarón, who worked on it for over two decades until his death in 2013.

**Carioca Aqueduct (Arcos da Lapa)**
An 18th-century colonial aqueduct with double-tiered arches in Lapa. Its top now carries the tracks of the historic Santa Teresa tram (bonde), which climbs to the hilltop Santa Teresa neighborhood.

**Petrobras and Vale headquarters**
Rio is home to the headquarters of Petrobras, Brazil's state-controlled oil company, and Vale, one of the world's largest mining companies.
